questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Distributive Law
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the distributive law

$$
CB-CA=C(B-A).
$$

So, compute $B-A$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}B-A & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 4 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =-3{I}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}CB-CA & =C(B-A) \\  & =C(-3{I}_{3}) \\  & =-3C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We apply the distributive law 

$$
AB+AC=A(B+C).
$$

So, we calculate $B+C$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}B+C & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -3 & 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={I}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}AB+AC & =A(B+C) \\  & =A{I}_{3} \\  & =A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, recall the associative law

$$
ABC=(AB)C=A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix, $B$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix, and $C$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $2\times 1$ matrix, which will require finding $2$ entries, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $3\times 2$ matrix, which will require finding $6$ entries.

So, we find the product $AB$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & -2 \\ -3 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $AB$ by $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =(AB)C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 15 \\ 3 & -9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Matrix Multiplication
questions.problem:
Given that $A$ and $B$  are $8\times 8$ matrices,  and ${I}_{8}$ is the $8\times 8$ identity matrix,  which of the following statements are always true?

- $A{I}_{8}={I}_{8}A$
- $AB=BA$
- $A\cdot 2{I}_{8}=2A$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general, however, multiplication by the identity matrix is always commutative. In this case, we have  $A{I}_{8}={I}_{8}A=A.$

- Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so $AB\ne BA$ in general.

- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so 

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot 2{I}_{8} & =A({I}_{8}+{I}_{8}) \\  & =A{I}_{8}+A{I}_{8} \\  & =A+A \\  & =2A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only statements I  and III are true.

Therefore, only statements II and III are true.

$$

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $3 \times 3$ matrix that will require finding $9$ entries, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $3 \times 1$ matrix that will require finding only $3$ entries.

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

- Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is associative, so $(AB)C = A(BC)$ in general.

- Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $A(B+C) = AB + AC$ in general. However, since matrix multiplication is not commutative, we have

$$
AB + AC  \neq BA + CA.
$$

- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $(A+B)C = AC+BC,$ and $A(B+C) = AB+AC$ in general.

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.
